title: Definitions Summary
text:
Observed DOI-linked scope
The report analyzes policy-document references that can be linked to scholarly works through DOIs. References without a DOI link are outside the analysis sample. The policy-document input is the project-provided dump_20250211.tar.gz archive dated 11 February 2025. Because the upstream Overton export query and selection criteria are not recoverable from this repository, the 97.6% document-level statistic is conditional on the provided dump and is not an estimate of coverage of the full Overton index.

title: Definitions Summary
section: Share of works cited by multiple policy documents
text:
Share of works cited by multiple policy documents
This measure is the share of distinct scholarly works cited by more than one policy document. In the baseline data, 48.1% of unique cited works are cited by at least two different policy documents.
This value applies only to the observed DOI-linked citation scope.

title: Definitions Summary
section: Share of citations to same-country research
text:
Share of citations to same-country research
This measure describes citations to research from the same country as the policy source. For each policy source country, it is the share of citations to research assigned to that country based on first-author affiliation. First-author country means the country of the first author’s affiliated institution, not the author’s nationality.
The country assignment first uses the standardized first-author country mode. If that is unavailable, it uses a single unambiguous two-letter raw country code. Works remain unassigned when neither step yields a country. This metric uses only citations assigned a first-author country under that sequential rule. It is therefore better used as a diagnostic than as a simple country ranking.

title: Definitions Summary
section: Expected share of citations to research from the same country
text:
Expected share of citations to research from the same country
The expected share combines the field mix of cited research with each country’s share of unique cited works within each field of the DOI-linked sample. Country refers to first-author affiliation. In this reference distribution, each unique cited work is counted once in each of its assigned domains. It is a descriptive reference based on the linked sample. It is not a model-based forecast, a target, or a measure of total global research production in OpenAlex.

title: Definitions Summary
section: Citations with and without an assigned research country
text:
Citations with and without an assigned research country
For Korean policy documents, 23,943 of 32,935 DOI-linked citations are assigned a research country; 8,992 (27.3%) remain unassigned and are reported separately. The unassigned share is 28.7% for KDI, 24.2% for KIEP, and 15.4% for other institutions. Placing all unassigned citations in the non-U.S. or U.S. category gives mechanical bounds of 40.1%–67.4% for the U.S. share. These are not model-based intervals. Country-level interpretation should therefore use the denominator stated for citations with an assigned research country.

title: Definitions Summary
section: Policy-source composition of Korea’s field gap
text:
Policy-source composition of Korea’s field gap
The social-science share is 77.9% for research cited by Korean policy documents, 40.3 percentage points above the 37.6% share in the full linked sample calculated with the same rule. The share is 23.1% for Korean research cited by policy documents, producing a 54.8-point gap between the two Korea-related directions. These shares count each assigned domain once per citation. A symmetric two-group decomposition attributes 38.2 percentage points to the mix of think-tank and non-think-tank sources and 16.6 points to differences within those source groups.
KDI and KIEP documents account for 71.4% of all Korean policy documents, 71.5% of DOI-citing documents, and 93.5% of DOI-linked citations in the Korean-policy-document direction. Their DOI-citing documents average 15.8 citations, compared with 2.7 for other institutions. Think tanks account for 93.6% in that direction, compared with 12.1% among policy documents citing Korean research. These are descriptive composition results, not causal estimates or intrinsic national preferences.
The social-science gap remains positive under alternative weighting rules: 58.4 percentage points with unique-work weighting, 32.2 points with equal policy-document weighting, and 59.9 points with fractional domain weighting, compared with 54.8 points in the primary analysis. These values answer different descriptive questions and do not form a single uncertainty interval.

title: Definitions Summary
section: Foreign think-tank distribution and citation-profile matches
text:
Foreign think-tank distribution and citation-profile matches
Korea has the highest think-tank citation share among the 11 report comparison countries. Within Korean think-tank citations, KDI and KIEP account for 99.9%. The foreign comparison sample contains 748 think tanks across 74 countries. Its median social-science share is 62.6% (range: 1.2%–96.0%). KDI and KIEP have shares of 82.1% and 86.0%, placing them at the 91.3rd and 96.4th percentiles.
The top 25 citation-profile matches span 17 countries: four are in the UK, three in the USA, two each in Belgium, France, and Germany, and one each in 12 other countries. Their median social-science share is 78.5%, but this is not an independent replication because the same cited-topic information is used to select the matches and calculate the field shares. Korea’s country-level result combines high institution-level social-science shares with concentration of observed DOI-linked citations in those two institutions. Source-type or citation-profile similarity does not establish equivalent legal status, mandates, or organizational roles.

title: Methods Summary
text:
Analysis scope

Data sources: Overton policy-document references and OpenAlex scholarly-work metadata.
Analysis input: the project-provided archive dump_20250211.tar.gz, dated 11 February 2025, with 1,471,454 parsed rows. The upstream Overton export query and selection criteria are not recoverable from this report repository, so document-level coverage statistics are conditional on that dump.
Citation unit: one policy document citing one OpenAlex work through a DOI. Multiple references to the same work within one document count once.
Document unit: distinct Overton policy document IDs.
Country comparisons assign the country of the first author’s affiliated institution, not the author’s nationality. The assignment first uses the most frequent standardized affiliation country code. When that code is unavailable, it uses a raw country code only if the available codes agree on one two-letter code.

title: Methods Summary
text:
Interpretation boundaries

The analysis covers observed DOI-linked policy-to-research citations, not every policy document or form of evidence.
Non-DOI evidence such as reports, legislation, web pages, and narrative references is outside the default indicators.
Hierarchical policy-source labels are collapsed to their top-level country, IGO, or EU category. The policy-source country is the country assigned to the organization that published the policy document. The IGO and EU categories are not countries, but they are compared at the same top level as source countries. Policy-source type labels can still overlap, so type totals are not mutually exclusive.
Works remain unassigned when neither the primary country rule nor the fallback yields a country. A missing or conflicting raw country code does not override a country assigned by the primary rule. For Korean policy documents, 23,943 of 32,935 DOI-linked citations are assigned a research country; 8,992 (27.3%) remain unassigned.
The unassigned share differs by institution: 28.7% for KDI, 24.2% for KIEP, and 15.4% for other institutions. Assigning all unassigned citations to non-U.S. or U.S. research gives mechanical bounds of 40.1%–67.4% for the U.S. share; these are not model-based intervals.

title: Methods Summary
text:
Denominator check
Do not compare indicator values until the denominator is clear. Check whether the denominator counts DOI-linked citations, unique works, policy documents, or only citations with an assigned research country. These units answer different questions.

title: Methods Summary
section: Source-composition decomposition of Korea’s field gap
text:
Source-composition decomposition of Korea’s field gap
The report separates the 54.8 percentage-point social-science share gap between the two Korea-related citation directions into two descriptive components. Policy documents are grouped into think tank and non-think-tank sources. A calculation that treats the two directions symmetrically attributes 38.2 percentage points to differences in source-type composition and 16.6 points to differences in social-science shares within source-type groups. These are arithmetic components, not causal effects.
The calculation uses four-domain citation assignments, counting a citation at most once within the same domain. Every policy document in the two relevant direction-specific samples has exactly one top-level source type. The decomposition locates where the observed gap appears; it does not estimate a causal effect or an intrinsic national preference.

title: Methods Summary
section: Foreign think-tank distribution and citation-profile matches
text:
Foreign think-tank distribution and citation-profile matches
For the institution-level comparison, foreign candidates must be tagged as think tanks in Overton and have at least 500 cited-topic assignments. The main distribution includes all 748 eligible institutions across 74 countries. Social-science shares use four-domain citation assignments, counting a citation at most once within the same domain. Separately, each candidate’s cited-topic frequency vector is compared with KDI and KIEP using cosine similarity. The two similarities receive equal weight, and the top 25 candidates are reported as nearest profile examples.
The field similarity of the top 25 matches is not an independent validation: the same cited-topic information is used to select the institutions and calculate their field shares. Neither the broad source-type comparison nor the profile ranking establishes that the institutions have the same legal status, policy mandate, or organizational role as KDI or KIEP.

title: Methods Summary
text:
Weighting sensitivity and institutional concentration
Under the main method, each assigned domain is counted once per citation and the Korea social-science gap is 54.8 percentage points. The gap is 58.4 points when unique works are counted, 32.2 points when policy documents receive equal weight, and 59.9 points when each citation’s weight is split across its domains. These results show sensitivity to the choice of unit and weighting method; they do not form a confidence interval.
KDI and KIEP account for 71.4% of all Korean policy documents, 71.5% of documents citing research through DOIs, and 93.5% of DOI-linked citations. Their documents with DOI-linked citations average 15.8 citations, compared with 2.7 for other institutions.

title: English Summary
text:
Analysis summary
The report examines DOI-linked citations from policy documents in Overton to scholarly works in OpenAlex. It does not measure every policy document or every form of evidence. It describes the observed citations from policy documents to research in the 2025 linked sample.
Prior studies show that citation counts from policy documents do not simply reproduce scholarly citation rankings. Policy documents cite a selective subset of research, with differences by field and document type, and article-level counts can have a low correlation with scholarly citations. The report uses this literature as an interpretive starting point; it does not directly compare scholarly citation counts with citations from policy documents for Korean research.
The report compares the policy sources that cite Korean research with the research countries and fields cited by Korean policy documents. Research country refers to the first author’s institutional affiliation, not nationality. Among citations from Korean policy documents with an assigned research country, U.S. research accounts for 55.2%. Its expected share based on the linked sample is 36.1%. This reference combines the cited field mix with each country’s share of unique works within each field. It does not use total OpenAlex research output.
Research country could not be assigned for 27.3% of citations from Korean policy documents. Assigning all of these citations to non-U.S. or U.S. research gives mechanical bounds of 40.1%–67.4% for the U.S. share. These are not confidence intervals.
Korea has the largest sum of absolute differences across the four domains among the 11 countries compared. The analysis also shows how the sample’s sources are composed. The Korea Development Institute (KDI) and the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP) account for 71.5% of Korean policy documents with DOI-linked citations and 93.5% of those citations. Much of the social-science gap between the two directions appears in the mix of policy source types. The gap remains positive under alternative weighting methods, ranging from 32.2 to 59.9 percentage points. These observations do not establish an intrinsic national preference.
The foreign comparison includes 748 eligible think tanks across 74 countries. Their median social-science share is 62.6%. KDI’s 82.1% and KIEP’s 86.0% place them at the 91.3rd and 96.4th percentiles, respectively, within the observed foreign range.

title: October 2026 Data Update
section: Comparing observed and expected country shares
text:
Comparing observed and expected country shares
Both shares use the same 308,842 citations from Korean policy documents with a research country and domain assigned. Of the citations with an assigned research country, 28 have no domain and are excluded from this comparison.
To calculate the expected share, we split each citation’s weight equally across its assigned domains, giving each citation a total weight of one. We then combine this domain mix with the country distribution of unique cited works within each domain of the linked sample. Only works with an assigned research country contribute to that reference distribution.
Among these citations, the observed share of U.S. research is 45.4% and the expected share is 35.1%, a difference of 10.3 percentage points. The expected share is a descriptive reference based on the linked sample’s field and country composition. It does not measure total OpenAlex research output or specify a policy target.
Figure 1 uses all citations with an assigned research country, including those without domains. The alternative calculations, domain weights, country distributions within domains and comparison sample counts document how the two shares were calculated.

title: October 2026 Data Update
text:
Data linkage and comparability

8,386,474 of 8,767,042 unique DOIs match OpenAlex. The 104,964 DOIs mapping to multiple work IDs are excluded from the primary analysis; an unrestricted-mapping sensitivity table is available.
The first author’s affiliation determines research country. We select the ROR country code that occurs most often across affiliation records; ties are broken alphabetically by country code. When no ROR country is available, we use an OpenAlex institution country only if the available codes agree on a single country. Works that cannot be assigned a country remain unassigned.
The 2025 baseline used a different fallback field. Snapshot coverage, DOI disambiguation and the fallback field all changed, so differences from the baseline must not be interpreted directly as behavioral trends.
Recent works were published in 2023–2025. Their share is calculated among cited works with a known publication year through 2025. The incomplete 2026 publication year is excluded. The baseline instead used 2022–2024.
Policy-source tags may overlap; citation counts do not measure causal policy impact.

section: Additional inputs for a full rebuild
text:
Additional inputs for a full rebuild
A complete rebuild from source data requires licensed Overton policy-document and DOI-citation records, policy-source country and type metadata, and OpenAlex work, authorship, and topic data aligned to the report snapshot. The code archive’s Data_Insight/Report/Report_Runbook.md records the expected paths and build order. Credentials and local-only notebooks are not included.

title: Public Reproducibility
text:
Environment and version identification
The baseline environment uses Python 3.12, Quarto 1.4.550, Pandoc 3.1.3, and Google Chrome 150. Exact Python package versions are recorded in the environment list and manifest. The manuscript publication date is 2025-12-31, the aggregate run tag is 20251026, and the data snapshots are Overton 2025.02 and OpenAlex 2025.06.
